pr.title: Simple validation for unsize coercion in MIR validation
pr.description:
This adds the most basic validity check to unsize coercions in MIR. The src and target of an unsize cast must *at least* implement `Src: CoerceUnsized<Target>` for this to be valid.

This doesn't the second, more subtle validity check that is taken of advantage in codegen [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/914193c8f40528fe82696e1054828de8c399882e/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/base.rs#L126), but I did leave a beefy FIXME for that explaining what it is.

As a consequence, this also fixes an ICE with GVN and invalid unsize coercions. This is somewhat coincidental, since MIR inlining will check that a body is valid before inlining it; so now that we determine it to be invalid, we don't inline it, and we don't encounter the GVN ICE. I'm not certain if the same GVN ICE is triggerable without the inliner, and perhaps instead with trivial where clauses or something.

cc @RalfJung
pr.author: compiler-errors

processing.reason: This PR is a missing-validation fix, not a wrong code transformation: no valid, defined Rust program changes behavior. The affected program relies on an ill-formed `impl<T, U> CastTo<U> for T` and an unsize coercion `&T -> &U` that does not satisfy `T: CoerceUnsized<U>`; modern rustc rejects it with E0277, and before the fix MIR validation merely failed to reject invalid MIR (the downstream GVN ICE is a consequence, not a miscompiled value). Constructing an "original vs transformed" function pair would therefore require either encoding invalid MIR/unsafe operations unrelated to the historical change or manufacturing a return-value difference in a program the patch never reinterprets. Both functions must pass Miri on concrete inputs, and no source-grounded pair with differing defined executions exists here.

analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect behavior was an omission in validation: an unsize coercion (`PointerCoercion::Unsize`) whose source and target types do not satisfy the `CoerceUnsized` trait was accepted as valid MIR. Because MIR inlining checks body validity before inlining, this invalid body was eligible to be inlined, and then GVN tried to evaluate the invalid unsize `() -> [i32]`, producing an ICE. The PR description states: "As a consequence, this also fixes an ICE with GVN and invalid unsize coercions. This is somewhat coincidental, since MIR inlining will check that a body is valid before inlining it; so now that we determine it to be invalid, we don't inline it, and we don't encounter the GVN ICE." Note this is a missing-validation bug, not a wrong rewrite: no valid program output changes; the fix rejects invalid MIR rather than altering a correct transform.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR bodies containing an unsize coercion cast, i.e. `CastKind::PointerCoercion(PointerCoercion::Unsize, _)`, where the operand type `op_ty` and target type `target_type` do not implement `Src: CoerceUnsized<Target>`. This can arise through an ill-formed trait bound/impl such as a `CastTo<U>: Unsize<U>` trait with a blanket `impl<T, U> CastTo<U> for T {}`, plus a generic method performing `let x: &U = self;`. Running with MIR inlining enabled makes the invalid body an inlining candidate; running GVN afterward triggers evaluation of the invalid unsize. The regression test uses `().cast::<[i32]>()` (unit to slice) with `-Zmir-opt-level=0 -Zmir-enable-passes=+Inline,+GVN -Zvalidate-mir`.
analysis.summary: Bug-fix PR: MIR validation previously did not check `PointerCoercion::Unsize` casts at all, so invalid unsize coercions (types not satisfying `CoerceUnsized`) passed validation. Adding the `CoerceUnsized` obligation check makes the MIR invalid, which prevents `Inline` from inlining it, which in turn avoids a downstream `GVN` ICE from evaluating an invalid unsize such as `() -> [i32]`. Also adds a debug assertion in codegen that a NOP trait-object upcast preserves the principal trait ref.
analysis.trigger: An unsize coercion cast appears in MIR without `Src: CoerceUnsized<Target>` holding; with Inline + GVN enabled, the invalid body is inlined and GVN attempts to process the invalid unsize cast (e.g. `() -> [i32]`), causing an ICE. After the fix, `Validator` rejects the body first so it is not inlined.
preconditions: A MIR `CastKind::PointerCoercion(PointerCoercion::Unsize, _)` whose operand/target do not satisfy the `CoerceUnsized` lang-item trait
Inlining enabled such that the invalid body is an inline candidate (the PR uses `+Inline`)
GVN enabled to observe the downstream invalid-unsize evaluation (the PR uses `+GVN`)
pitfalls: Do not treat this as an optimization rewrite bug: the validator simply lacked a check; no valid program's transformed output changes.
The GVN ICE is a downstream consequence, not evidence that GVN's rewrite is wrong; the invalid MIR should never have passed validation or been inlined.
The check must use `predicate_must_hold_modulo_regions` / an obligation, not a syntactic pointer check, because `Unsize` applies to all `CoerceUnsized` types, not just pointers/references.

The codegen NOP-upcast assumption (`data_a.principal_def_id() == data_b.principal_def_id()`) additionally assumes equal principal trait refs; a debug assertion was added, but the second more subtle codegen validity check remains a FIXME and is not covered by this validation.
Merely checking that the source/target are pointer-like is insufficient; the actual `CoerceUnsized` bound must be proven.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a UI test under `tests/ui/mir/validate/` with `-Zmir-opt-level=0 -Zmir-enable-passes=+Inline,+GVN -Zvalidate-mir` and `#![feature(unsize)]`. Define `pub trait CastTo<U: ?Sized>: Unsize<U> {}` with the intentionally not-well-formed blanket `impl<T: ?Sized, U: ?Sized> CastTo<U> for T {}`, and `impl<T: ?Sized> Cast for T` whose `cast` body does `let x: &U = self;`. In `main`, call `().cast::<[i32]>()` so inlining would expose a `() -> [i32]` unsize to GVN. Check the emitted diagnostic (`the trait bound T: Unsize<U> is not satisfied`, E0277) via the `.stderr` file. Also update/remove the old `tests/crashes/129219.rs` known-bug test that this fixes.
